lesson.title: Skipping the Sum: Evaluating Integrals Without a Limit
lesson.summary: The second part of the fundamental theorem says the definite integral of f from a to b equals F(b) minus F(a) for any antiderivative F of f, turning an infinite limiting process into two evaluations and a subtraction.
lesson.body:
Part one of the fundamental theorem showed that the accumulation function F(x) = the integral from a to x of f(t) dt satisfies F'(x) = f(x), meaning F is one particular antiderivative of f. Part two pushes this further and asks: what if you use a different antiderivative, one you already happen to know, instead of building the accumulation function from scratch? The answer is that it does not matter which antiderivative you use. If G is any function at all with G'(x) = f(x) on [a, b], then the integral from a to b of f(x) dx equals G(b) - G(a).

The reason any antiderivative works is a fact about antiderivatives themselves: if G'(x) = f(x) and the accumulation function F also satisfies F'(x) = f(x), then G and F have the same derivative everywhere on the interval, which means they differ by a constant, G(x) = F(x) + C for some fixed C. When you compute G(b) - G(a), that constant cancels: G(b) - G(a) = [F(b) + C] - [F(a) + C] = F(b) - F(a). So no matter which antiderivative you reach for, the difference G(b) - G(a) always gives the same number, and that number is the definite integral. This is what makes the theorem a genuine shortcut: you are free to pick whichever antiderivative is easiest to write down.

Here is a worked example. Let f(x) = 2x on [2, 5]. An antiderivative of 2x is x^2, so by part two, the integral from 2 to 5 of 2x dx = 5^2 - 2^2 = 25 - 4 = 21. Check this against plain geometry: f(x) = 2x is a line, so the region under it on [2, 5] is a trapezoid with parallel sides f(2) = 4 and f(5) = 10 and width 3, giving area (4 + 10)/2 times 3 = 21. The antiderivative shortcut and the direct geometric area agree exactly, but notice how much less work the shortcut took: no Riemann sum, no limit, just one antiderivative and a subtraction.

That is the real power of this half of the fundamental theorem. Every earlier worked example in this chapter sequence that used a Riemann sum and a limit to grind out a definite integral could instead have been solved in two lines: find any antiderivative, evaluate it at the two limits of integration, and subtract. The next chapter turns this into a concrete, repeatable procedure.
